prompt_free_text:
This paper proposes a two-stage approach for EEG-to-text decoding from text-evoked EEG: a self-supervised pretraining model, CET-MAE, that combines EEG-text contrastive learning with masked reconstruction of both modalities, and a downstream decoding framework, E2T-PTR, that transfers the pretrained EEG-side representations into a BART-based generator. The paper also introduces a practical modification to the ZuCo input representation by concatenating sentence-level EEG features with word-level EEG features to mitigate missing fixation-induced corruption. Empirically, the method is evaluated on ZuCo under three-, four-, and five-task settings and is reported to outperform prior work on several BLEU and ROUGE metrics.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and reasonably timely. The idea of combining cross-modal alignment and intra-modal reconstruction for EEG-text representation learning is sensible, and the attempt to leverage pretrained language models more effectively for EEG decoding is well motivated. The paper also addresses a real issue in ZuCo, namely the incompleteness and misalignment of word-level EEG due to fixation gaps, and the sentence-level augmentation is a pragmatic design choice. The empirical results are promising, especially in the three-task and five-task settings. That said, I also have substantial concerns about experimental rigor, fairness of comparison, clarity of the task formulation, and the strength of the claimed contributions relative to what is actually demonstrated.

The main strength of the paper is the formulation of a multimodal SSL objective tailored to EEG-text pairs. The combination of masked text modeling, masked EEG modeling, and EEG-text contrastive learning is conceptually coherent, and the multi-stream encoder design is a plausible way to separate modality-specific and joint processing. The paper also does a decent job motivating why contrastive learning alone may miss fine-grained modality information and why masked modeling alone may underemphasize pairwise matching. The transfer setup into a BART-based decoder is also natural and likely useful in practice. In addition, the paper includes several ablations: with and without sentence-level EEG, with and without CET-MAE pretraining, and comparisons among CET, ET-MAE, and CET-MAE. These are helpful and support the claim that the hybrid SSL objective is better than either component alone, though the gains are modest.

However, the paper’s central empirical claims need to be interpreted more cautiously. The headline claim of outperforming SOTA by 8.34% ROUGE-1 F1 and 32.21% BLEU-4 appears to rely on selective comparisons across different dataset scales and possibly different evaluation conventions. In Table 1, the strongest prior method in the four-task setting, C-SCL, has much higher BLEU-3/4 than the proposed method, while the proposed method is only slightly better on BLEU-1/2 and roughly tied or slightly worse on ROUGE-1 F1 depending on whether one compares to C-SCL or C-SCL*. In the three-task setting, the gains over DeWave are real but modest in absolute terms. In the five-task setting, the comparison is only against EEG2Text*, not against stronger recent baselines. Therefore, the “state-of-the-art” claim should be qualified much more carefully by task setting, training sample count, and metric. As written, the abstract overstates the consistency and magnitude of the improvements.

A second major concern is evaluation fairness and reproducibility. The paper says it follows the preprocessing and splits of Wang and Ji (2022), but it also changes the input representation by concatenating sentence-level EEG with word-level EEG. This is a meaningful modification to the task input and likely contributes substantially to the gains. While Table 5 partially ablates sentence-level EEG, the comparisons to prior work are not fully apples-to-apples unless those baselines are reimplemented with the same augmented input. Similarly, the paper uses BART both as a frozen text encoder in pretraining and as a fully fine-tuned decoder in downstream training. It is not entirely clear whether the gains come primarily from the SSL pretraining, from the sentence-level EEG token, from architectural changes in the EEG encoder, or simply from stronger fine-tuning of BART. The ablations help, but they do not fully disentangle these factors.

Relatedly, the transfer gains from CET-MAE over CET and ET-MAE in Table 6 are quite small: roughly 0.3 to 0.5 BLEU points and less than 1 ROUGE point. These improvements may still matter in this difficult domain, but the paper does not report variance across runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Given the small dataset and likely high variance of sequence generation metrics, it is difficult to know whether these differences are robust. This is especially important because the paper makes strong claims about the superiority of the hybrid SSL objective. At minimum, the authors should report mean and standard deviation over multiple seeds and ideally perform paired significance testing on generation outputs.

The task formulation also raises some conceptual concerns. The paper acknowledges reliance on “implicit teacher forcing,” but this issue is more serious than the limitations section suggests. If the model uses aligned word-level EEG segments derived from eye fixations during reading of the target sentence, then the decoding problem is not equivalent to unconstrained language production from brain activity. It is closer to reconstructing or translating a sentence that the subject is currently reading, with strong temporal alignment to the text. This is still a valid and interesting task, but the paper occasionally frames it in broader BCI terms that may overstate practical implications. The distinction between text-evoked EEG during reading and intended speech/language decoding should be made much more explicitly throughout the paper.

There are also several methodological details that are underspecified. The paper says the text tokens are processed with BERT in Section 3.2, but Section 3.3 says the text encoder is BART. This inconsistency is confusing. The exact form of the contrastive loss is not given: temperature, normalization, in-batch negatives, symmetric or asymmetric objective, and whether the pooled representations come from masked or unmasked positions are all omitted. The masking strategy for EEG is unusual, especially compulsory masking of sentence-level EEG, but the rationale is only partly convincing and the implementation details are unclear. Are sentence-level EEG features always entirely masked during pretraining? If so, how is the model prevented from simply learning to reconstruct them from text alone? More generally, because the paired text is available during pretraining, the reconstruction objectives may encourage shortcut learning from text to EEG and vice versa rather than robust EEG semantics. Some analysis of cross-modal dependence would strengthen the paper.

The architecture description is also not fully satisfactory. The EEG encoder is described as a transformer over EEG tokens with “spatial and frequency features in each token,” but the exact EEG feature representation is not specified in the main text. Since performance in EEG tasks is highly sensitive to preprocessing and feature extraction, this omission is important. The dimensions are also surprisingly large relative to dataset size: 2048 hidden dimensions in the EEG encoder and 4096 in the multi-stream transformer seem potentially overparameterized for ZuCo-scale data. It would be useful to know parameter counts, training stability, and whether smaller models perform similarly. Without this, it is hard to assess whether the method is efficient or likely to generalize.

The qualitative examples are mixed. Some examples do show improved grammaticality and phrase-level recovery, but they also reveal substantial hallucination and poor named entity decoding. In fact, several outputs appear to preserve broad sentence templates while failing on content words, especially names and locations. This suggests the model may rely heavily on language-model priors and dataset regularities rather than precise EEG-derived lexical information. The paper acknowledges named entity failures, but this deserves deeper analysis. For example, reporting content-word accuracy, named entity accuracy, or calibration of lexical uncertainty would be more informative than BLEU/ROUGE alone. Given the strong language prior from BART, n-gram overlap metrics may overestimate actual brain-decoding fidelity.

Another concern is the lack of stronger baselines and broader evaluation. Since the paper’s main novelty is multimodal pretraining, it would be important to compare against simpler transfer baselines such as EEG encoder pretraining with only masked EEG modeling, only sentence-level augmentation without multimodal pretraining, or direct fine-tuning of BART with the same EEG encoder but random initialization. Some of these are partially covered, but not comprehensively. It would also be valuable to compare against non-generative retrieval-style evaluations, such as whether the EEG representation can identify the correct sentence among distractors. Such analyses would better isolate semantic alignment quality from language-model generation effects.

The paper’s writing is understandable overall, but there are many grammatical issues, inconsistencies, and overclaims. Examples include “our goal L is minimizing,” “specialized head for each modality,” and inconsistent references to BERT versus BART. The presentation of Table 1 is also somewhat confusing because it mixes different sample counts and evaluation conventions, including parenthetical scores with repeated words retained. The paper would benefit from a cleaner separation of settings and a more disciplined comparison protocol. The ethics statement is minimal and somewhat too dismissive; while the work uses public data, brain decoding research does raise privacy and misuse considerations, even if current capabilities are limited.

In terms of novelty, I would characterize the contribution as moderate rather than high. Combining contrastive alignment and masked autoencoding is by now a standard multimodal pretraining pattern, and the paper adapts this recipe to EEG-text data. That adaptation is worthwhile, and perhaps the first of its kind in this exact setting, but the conceptual leap is not large. The more distinctive practical contribution may actually be the sentence-level EEG augmentation and the transfer recipe into BART. The paper should position itself more as a careful domain adaptation of multimodal SSL to EEG-text decoding rather than as a fundamentally new learning paradigm.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following. First, report multi-seed results with standard deviations and significance tests for all main comparisons. Second, clarify the exact evaluation settings and avoid aggregating claims across incomparable task/sample regimes. Third, provide a more rigorous ablation isolating the effects of sentence-level EEG, SSL pretraining, and BART fine-tuning. Fourth, specify all missing methodological details, especially EEG feature construction, contrastive loss formulation, masking implementation, and parameter counts. Fifth, add analyses beyond BLEU/ROUGE, particularly content-word or named-entity accuracy, retrieval accuracy, and perhaps human evaluation of semantic fidelity. Sixth, tone down claims about broad BCI applicability and clearly distinguish text-evoked reading EEG from general language decoding.

My overall assessment is that this is a promising paper with a sensible method and encouraging results, but the current version falls short of the rigor expected for a top-tier ML venue. The empirical gains are not yet established robustly enough, the comparisons are not fully clean, and several methodological details remain unclear. With stronger experimental validation and clearer framing, this could become a solid contribution to multimodal learning for neural decoding.

If I were making a recommendation, it would be borderline leaning negative for a top-tier conference in its current form, primarily due to concerns about evaluation rigor and overstatement, but I do think the work has merit and could be improved substantially with revision.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes CET-MAE, a self-supervised EEG-text pretraining model that combines masked reconstruction for both modalities with EEG-text contrastive learning via a multi-stream transformer, and E2T-PTR, a downstream EEG-to-text framework that transfers the pretrained EEG-side representations into a BART-based generator. Experiments on ZuCo reading-task combinations report improvements over prior EEG-to-text systems on BLEU and ROUGE metrics, with ablations suggesting benefits from combining sentence-level EEG features, pretraining, and the joint SSL objective.
strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: open-vocabulary EEG-to-text decoding from non-invasive recordings.
The proposed pretraining objective is intuitively motivated, combining cross-modal alignment and intra-modal reconstruction, which is a reasonable design for multimodal representation learning.
The paper evaluates on multiple ZuCo task combinations (three, four, and five reading tasks) rather than a single split, which broadens empirical coverage.
Includes several ablations: masking ratios, component removal, and comparison among contrastive-only, MAE-only, and combined SSL variants.
Qualitative examples and discussion of failure modes (especially named entities) are useful and candid.
weaknesses: The empirical gains over the strongest baselines are often modest in absolute terms, especially in the more directly comparable settings; the headline percentage improvements appear selectively framed and may overstate practical significance.

Experimental comparability is weak: some baselines use different sample counts, some are reproduced by the authors, and evaluation protocols differ regarding repeated-token removal, making SOTA claims less convincing.
No statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or multi-seed variance are reported, which is especially problematic given the small absolute improvements and small dataset scale.

The paper does not clearly disentangle how much of the gain comes from the proposed SSL pretraining versus simpler changes such as adding sentence-level EEG features, using BART, or scaling training data.

Method details are insufficient for rigorous reproducibility: exact contrastive loss formulation, pooling details, masking implementation, optimization hyperparameters, and how EEG/text lengths are handled are under-specified.

The scientific framing around 'teacher forcing' is confusing and potentially misleading; the paper suggests test-time implicit access to ground-truth tokens, which is not a standard or acceptable description for a decoding task and raises concerns about evaluation clarity.
The paper makes strong claims about semantic decoding and BCI potential, but the qualitative outputs still show substantial hallucination and poor named-entity fidelity, limiting practical impact.
There is no evaluation of cross-subject generalization robustness, subject-wise variance, or whether gains hold consistently across tasks/subjects, which is crucial for EEG decoding.
methodological_flaws: The statement in Section 3.1 that during testing the model 'operates with an implicit understanding of the ground-truth word tokens W' is scientifically problematic. If ground-truth tokens are used in any way at inference, the evaluation would be invalid; if not, the description is incorrect and reflects serious ambiguity in the experimental protocol.

The comparison tables mix results from different training sample sizes and partially reproduced baselines, yet the paper still makes broad superiority claims. This weakens empirical validity because improvements may be confounded by data scale and implementation differences rather than method quality.

The reported improvements lack statistical testing across random seeds. Given gains such as ~0.3-0.5 BLEU in several ablations, it is impossible to know whether the effects are robust or within training variance.

The masking-ratio conclusion is based on a narrow trial-and-error sweep without controlling for other factors or reporting variance; claiming that 75% 'can achieve the best results' is not sufficiently supported.

The ablation design does not fully isolate the contribution of CET-MAE pretraining from architectural changes in E2T-PTR. For example, adding sentence-level EEG features and transferring pretrained modules are changed together across some comparisons, so causal attribution is incomplete.

The paper provides no mathematical analysis or proof for why the multi-stream architecture avoids 'erroneous learning processes' or misleading contrastive feedback; these are asserted rather than demonstrated.

Using BLEU/ROUGE alone for this task is limited, especially when outputs can be semantically plausible but lexically different or can exploit repetitive patterns. The paper does not include complementary semantic or human evaluation to validate decoding quality.

The claim of 'comprehensive experiments' is overstated because key baselines such as stronger recent multimodal or EEG representation learners are not uniformly reimplemented under a single controlled protocol.
